overview: The ESP32 is a dual-core WiFi + Bluetooth system-on-chip that costs about the same as an Arduino Nano but runs roughly ten times faster and can talk to the internet natively — no add-on shield required. It's the board most people upgrade to once an Uno-class project needs networking, more processing headroom, or Bluetooth. The catch is that its logic is strictly 3.3V (unlike the Uno's more forgiving 5V), and a handful of pins have quirky boot-time behavior that can silently break a project if you don't know about them. Variants like the ESP32-S3 (adds native USB, more GPIO) and ESP32-C3 (single-core RISC-V, cheaper, smaller) share the same core ideas with different pin counts.
simpleSummary: A cheap microcontroller with built-in WiFi and Bluetooth, faster than an Arduino.

specifications.microcontroller: Xtensa dual-core LX6, up to 240 MHz
specifications.adc: 12-bit, ADC1 (GPIO32-39) usable alongside WiFi, ADC2 pins conflict with WiFi

pinMap.name: 3V3
pinMap.function: Regulated 3.3V output from the onboard regulator.
pinMap.currentLimit: ~600 mA shared, less under WiFi transmit bursts
pinMap.gotcha: WiFi transmit bursts can draw 400-500mA spikes — a weak USB port or breadboard power rail causes random reboots.

pinMap.name: VIN
pinMap.function: 5V input, feeds the onboard 3.3V regulator (often labeled 5V on some boards).

pinMap.name: EN
pinMap.function: Chip enable / reset. Pulling LOW resets the module.

pinMap.name: GPIO0
pinMap.function: General-purpose I/O, also the BOOT button pin that selects normal-boot vs flashing mode at power-on.
pinMap.gotcha: Must be HIGH at boot for normal operation; if a connected component pulls it LOW, the board can get stuck failing to boot your program.

pinMap.name: GPIO1 (TX0)
pinMap.function: Hardware serial transmit, also used by the USB-serial bridge for flashing/debugging.
pinMap.gotcha: Avoid using for general I/O if you need USB Serial output.

pinMap.name: GPIO3 (RX0)
pinMap.function: Hardware serial receive, shared with USB-serial bridge.
pinMap.gotcha: Must be HIGH at boot; something pulling it LOW can prevent flashing.

pinMap.name: GPIO2
pinMap.function: General-purpose I/O, often wired to an onboard LED on dev boards.
pinMap.gotcha: Must be LOW or floating at boot on some boards to enter flashing mode correctly.

pinMap.name: GPIO5
pinMap.function: General-purpose I/O, also an SPI chip-select on many boards.
pinMap.gotcha: Boot strapping pin — must be HIGH at boot.

pinMap.name: GPIO12
pinMap.gotcha: Boot strapping pin — pulling HIGH at boot can prevent the internal flash voltage from being set correctly. Best avoided for external pull-ups.

pinMap.name: GPIO15
pinMap.gotcha: Boot strapping pin controlling boot log verbosity — safe to use but avoid pulling LOW at boot.

pinMap.name: GPIO16
pinMap.gotcha: Unavailable on boards using this pin for PSRAM (some ESP32-WROVER modules).

pinMap.name: GPIO17
pinMap.gotcha: Same PSRAM caveat as GPIO16 on WROVER-based boards.

pinMap.name: GPIO25
pinMap.function: General-purpose I/O with true analog output (DAC).

pinMap.name: GPIO26
pinMap.function: General-purpose I/O with true analog output (DAC).

pinMap.name: GPIO32
pinMap.function: Analog input, usable alongside active WiFi.

pinMap.name: GPIO33
pinMap.function: Analog input, usable alongside active WiFi.

pinMap.name: GPIO34
pinMap.gotcha: Input-only — cannot drive an LED or any output, a frequent beginner surprise.

useCases.title: WiFi-connected sensor dashboard
useCases.scenario: Read a sensor and publish readings to a web dashboard or MQTT broker over WiFi — no separate networking shield needed.

useCases.title: Bluetooth-controlled robot
useCases.scenario: Drive a small robot's motors from a phone app over BLE instead of a dedicated Bluetooth module.

useCases.title: Battery-powered environment logger with deep sleep
useCases.scenario: Use the ESP32's deep-sleep modes to log temperature/humidity for months on a single battery charge, waking briefly to transmit.

useCases.title: Home automation node
useCases.scenario: Control relays and read sensors, integrating with Home Assistant / ESPHome over WiFi.

oftenConfusedWith: ESP8266/NodeMCU (WiFi only, no Bluetooth, single core)
oftenUpgradedTo: Raspberry Pi Zero W (when a full Linux OS is needed instead of a microcontroller RTOS)
